say: Welcome back, detectives! Someone has spilled ink on our sums and some digits have disappeared.
Today we find the missing digits, make both sides of "=" balance, and crack some magic squares. Notice it. Test it. Explain why.
I say a number. You say its partner to make 100. Ready? 65!
Now partners to 1000. 370! How did you find 630 so fast?
Pick any 3-digit number. I predict that its partner to make 999 will be easy to find, with no carrying at all. Do you think I am right? Let us test it.
stuck: Stuck: start with the hundreds. What goes with 3 to make 9?
Not sure: add your two numbers in a column sum to check the total is 999.
Finished early: try partners to 1000. What changes in the ones column?

say: “4[ ]7 + 28[ ] = 723. I start at the ones: 7 plus the ones box ends in 3. 7 + 6 = 13. So the ones box is 6, and I carry 1 ten.”
“Tens: the tens box + 8 + the carried 1 ends in 2. 3 + 8 + 1 = 12. So the tens box is 3, and I carry 1 hundred. Hundreds: 4 + 2 + 1 = 7. It matches! I check by adding: 437 + 286 = 723.”

“6[ ]2 − 24[ ] = 385. Subtraction is harder, so I work backwards and turn it into an addition: 385 + 24[ ] = 6[ ]2. Ones: 5 + the ones box ends in 2, 5 + 7 = 12, so it is 7. Tens: 8 + 4 + 1 = 13, so the tens box is 3. Hundreds: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 ✓.”
“245 + 130 = 200 + [ ]. I do not need to add. 245 is 45 more than 200, so the box must be 45 more than 130. That is 175. Both sides are 375.”

do: Ask: “Which column did you start with? Why?”
Ask: “Was there a carry into this column? How do you know?”
Ask: “What is each side of the = sign worth? Are they the same?”
stuck: Hint 2: “Try a digit in the box and add. Too big or too small?”
Hint 3: “Turn the subtraction into an addition: answer + bottom number = top number.”

do: Ask: “Which column did you start with? Why?”
Ask: “Was there a carry into this column? How do you know?”
Ask: “What is each side of the = sign worth? Are they the same?”
stuck: Hint 2: “Try a digit in the box and add. Too big or too small?”
Hint 3: “Turn the subtraction into an addition: answer + bottom number = top number.”

say: “Why do we start at the ones column when we look for missing digits?”
ask: “Why do we start at the ones column when we look for missing digits?”
The ones column can make a carry that changes the tens column, and the tens can change the hundreds, so we must know the ones first.

say: “You were digit detectives again: you started at the ones, checked every carry and proved each answer by adding.”

p2l2-title.note: Objective: Find missing digits in 3-digit addition and subtraction by starting at the ones and checking for a carry, use "=" as "is the same as" to balance number sentences, and complete magic squares and triangles with bigger numbers. Thinking strategies taught today: WORK BACKWARDS (turn a subtraction into an addition) and GUESS AND CHECK (try a digit, test it, improve). Also: draw a model for two numbers with a known total and difference. Materials: Digit cards 0 to 9, base-ten blocks or place-value counters, mini whiteboards, a paper magic triangle with 6 circles and number tiles 110 to 160. Online: children write column sums on whiteboards and say the answer together on three; number tiles are cut from paper before the lesson; the tutor writes on the slide sums. Time plan: opening 0 to 1.5, sneak-peek puzzles 1.5 to 6, warm-up 6 to 10.5, explore 10.5 to 23.5, mini-lesson 23.5 to 35.5, brain break 35.5 to 38.5, worksheet page 1 38.5 to 52.5, check together, page 1 52.5 to 55, short teaching 55 to 59.5, worksheet page 2 59.5 to 71, check together, page 2 71 to 73.5, flex (spare time) 73.5 to 76.5, talk time 76.5 to 81.5, exit ticket 81.5 to 86.5, looking back 86.5 to 88.5, closing and stamps 88.5 to 90. The Think harder and Go further slides are optional, if you finish early (no clock time). Kit ready at minute 0: ask families to put every item on the desk before the lesson starts (a 30-second check at the start).

p2l2-precheck.note: Minutes 1.5 to 6. Sneak-peek puzzles: two puzzles on the key idea of today, which the children have NOT learnt yet. Say out loud (about 28 words): "Two sneak-peek puzzles on ideas we have not learnt yet. Guessing is welcome, so is I do not know. Nobody is marked. Say your answer together on three." Question 1 is an access question: any child can try it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone has a first win (about 45 seconds). Question 2 is the thinking question (about 90 seconds). Then about 2 minutes for the answers slide and the move on. Answers are PRIVATE: each child writes on their own paper and says the answer together on three; nothing is held up to the camera. Do not raise whiteboards together, do not read answers out, do not name children. Q1 answer: 7 (372 + 416 = 788). Listen for: No carry in this one: look at the tens column, 1 and what makes 8. This is a first win for everyone. Q2 answer: 4 (446 + 237 = 683). Listen for: Ones: 6 + 7 = 13, so 1 ten is carried. Tens: the box + 3 + 1 must end in 8, so the box is 4. Listen for: "carry", or a guess that was tested and checked. At the end click to show the answers as "one way to think about it", without saying who had what. Ask only for volunteers: "Would anyone like to tell us how they started?" Invite the WHOLE group at once, never one child: "When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Never announce who is on which page. Pairs are not split unless both children agree. Children can move either way at any time. Everyone joins explore, the mini-lesson, the check-together slides and talk time.

p2l2-warm1.note: Minutes 6 to 8.5. Partners. Say a number; children call out the partner (online: unmute together or type in the chat). Click to reveal each answer, left column first. Spare calls if the children want more: 30, 85, 99 for 100; 600, 240, 505 for 1000. Do not run over: three calls are enough. Ask after 125: "How did you find 875 so fast?" Listen for: "1 and 8 make 9 hundreds, 2 and 7 make 9 tens, 5 and 5 make 10 ones." That is the key to today's explore. Watch for: children who say 985 for 125 (making every column 10). The columns are 9, 9 and 10 because of the carries. A game of about 2.5 minutes: stop it on the clock even if the game is not finished.

p2l2-warm2.note: Minutes 8.5 to 10.5. Write it, say the answer together on three, then click. For question 2 ask: "How did you take 250 from 700?" (700 − 200 = 500, then − 50 = 450). Answers: 35 and 450. Spare questions in the guide table: 300 + 450 = 750, 238 + 10 = 248, 500 − __ = 120 is 380 (count on: 120 → 200 is 80, 200 → 500 is 300). Ask quick questions 1 and 3 only (about 2 minutes): children answer by thumbs, hands, not by naming a child. The other questions are spare.

p2l2-explore1.note: Minutes 10.5 to 19.5. Pairs choose their own 3-digit numbers and find partners to 999, checking with a column sum. Do not explain the pattern; let them find it. Any child who would like more: "Now find partners to 1000. What changes?" (the ones add up to 10 and the tens and hundreds to 9, because of the carry). Go further (a second what-if, so nobody waits) is the box at the foot of this slide; the question is also posted in the chat when the pairs go to their breakout rooms. It is for ANY child who finishes the explore task or wants more: say it to the whole group as a choice, never as a prize, and never name who tries it. Pairs stay together unless both children agree to split. Answer: 642. Ones: 8 + 2 = 10. Tens: 5 + 4 + 1 = 10. Hundreds: 3 + 6 + 1 = 10. Every column carries. Take it at the debrief only if a pair offers it.

p2l2-explore2.note: Minutes 19.5 to 23.5. Gather the group. Answers: 1) The two digits in each column add up to 9. 2) No column adds up to more than 9, so nothing is carried. 3) 725 (2 + 7, 7 + 2 and 4 + 5 all make 9). Push: "So if I know the answer and one number, can I find a missing digit?" That is today's mystery. Keep it moving (about 4 minutes in all): ask "how do you know?" on question 2 only; about 15 seconds of talk on the other questions.

p2l2-teach1.note: Minutes 23.5 to 27.5. Teach. Ask first: "Which column should we start with?" Some children start at the hundreds: 4 + 2 = 6, not 7, and they get stuck. Show why the ones go first: a carry from the ones changes the tens, and a carry from the tens changes the hundreds. Think-aloud: "7 plus something ends in 3. 7 + 6 = 13. The box is 6, and I carry 1 ten. Tens: something + 8 + 1 ends in 2 …" Guess and check works too: "Try 2 in the tens box: 2 + 8 + 1 = 11. Ends in 1, not 2. Try 3." SUBTRACTION (this slide holds the old we2 slide as its last box): work backwards. Subtraction with gaps is hard, so undo it: 385 + 247 must make 632. Click to show the turned-round sum, then each step. Check the other way at the end: 632 − 247, ones 2 − 7 cannot be done, so take a ten: 12 − 7 = 5 ✓. The answer plus the number we took away gives back the number we started with.

p2l2-try1.note: Minutes 27.5 to 29.5. Write each as a column sum on the whiteboard first. a) No carries: 4 + 4 = 8. b) Ones: the first box + 7 ends in 2, so 5 (12, carry 1). Tens: 5 + the second box + 1 ends in 1, so 5 (11, carry 1). Hundreds 1 + 2 + 1 = 4 ✓: 155 + 257. (The old item c, [ ]64 + 17[ ] = 542, is dropped: the worksheet has the same type.)

p2l2-try2.note: Minutes 29.5 to 31. Whiteboards. One item only: 514 + 321 = 835, so the box is 3. Say it back in a sentence: "I turned it into an addition." (Items b and c are dropped: worksheet Q2 has the same type.)

p2l2-teach3.note: Minutes 31 to 34.5. Teach. Ask first: "What goes in the box?" Some children say 375 because "the answer comes next". The see-saw must balance: both sides the same. Click through. Two ways: compare (look for the difference between 245 and 200), or work out the full side and subtract. Comparing is faster with big numbers, and it is how Ravi's question on the worksheet works.

p2l2-key.note: Minutes 34.5 to 35.5. Say the key ideas together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Forgetting the carried 1: in Q1c writing 6 in the tens box (8 + 6 = 14) instead of 5 (8 + 5 + 1 = 14). (2) Reading "=" as "the answer comes next": 350 + 140 = 300 + [ ] answered 490. (3) Magic triangle: putting the biggest numbers in the corners when the side total is small.

p2l2-break.note: Minutes 35.5 to 38.5. Three minutes: two of movement, one for a drink of water. Sentences to call: 300 + 200 = 400 + 100 (true); 250 + 250 = 600 (false); 999 = 1000 − 1 (true); 450 + 50 = 400 + 150 (false). Online: children lean in front of the camera.

p2l2-ws1.note: Minutes 38.5 to 52.5. Walk around. Ask "Was there a carry into this column?" before giving any help. Q3 c and d and the line under Q1 (check one answer by adding) are marked ★ take-home on the page: children do them at home. Ravi's idea (Q3d) comes back at home, not in class. Say once, to everyone: "After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." Never say who is on which page. Invite the WHOLE group at once, never one child: "When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Pairs are not split unless both children agree.

p2l2-ws1ans.note: Minutes 52.5 to 55. Click each answer after a pair explains theirs. Q1b: ones 2 + 5 = 7 (no carry), tens 6 + 7 = 13, hundreds 4 + 3 + 1 = 8. Q1c: ones 6 + 9 = 15, tens 8 + 5 + 1 = 14, hundreds 3 + 2 + 1 = 6. Q2b: 276 + 267 = 543. Q3 c and d are take-home stars: the answers stay here so children can mark them at home (Q3d: both sides are 603; moving 2 from one number to the other does not change the total).

p2l2-teachsq.note: Minutes 55 to 57.5. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4). Click order: step 1, step 2, step 3, the check line, then the full square appears. Ask the group for the last two (210 and 230) before the square is shown. The worksheet square uses different numbers and asks what happens if we add 100 to every number: do not tell them.

p2l2-teachtwo.note: Minutes 57.5 to 59.5. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q6). Draw a model: the big bar is the small bar plus the extra. Take the extra away, share what is left into two equal bars, then give the extra back. Children who guess and check (250 and 250? 150 and 350?) are welcome: ask them to check BOTH clues. Halving 400: half of 4 hundreds is 2 hundreds.

p2l2-ws2.note: Minutes 59.5 to 71. Children work alone. Q5 (the magic triangle) is marked ★ take-home: it is done at home, and its teaching slide is not shown in class. Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson, especially anyone still starting column sums at the hundreds. Tutor rule at minute 59.5: if the clock is more than 2 minutes late, drop the last Core question of page 2 to take-home (children draw a star beside it). Never shorten talk time, the exit ticket, looking back or the closing. Questions marked with a star and the words take-home on the page are done at home; their answers are still on the check-together slide.

p2l2-ws2ans.note: Minutes 71 to 73.5. Click after a child explains (answer lines only). Q4c: every line has three numbers and each went up by 100, so every line total went up by 300. Q5a: 390 is the smallest total possible, so the smallest numbers are corners: 110 + 160 + 120, 120 + 140 + 130, 130 + 150 + 110. The side total 420 (corners 140, 150, 160) is Think harder 1. Q6 check: 250 + 450 = 700 and 450 − 250 = 200.

p2l2-stretch.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time). Open to any child who chooses it (the choice after question 3 on the worksheet). These are the SAME four questions as the printed Think harder page: the slide shows 1 to 3 and question 4 is on the page only. Never announce who is working on which page. Answers: 1) Corners 140, 150, 160. Between 140 and 150: 130. Between 150 and 160: 110. Between 160 and 140: 120 (each side: 140 + 130 + 150 = 420, 150 + 110 + 160 = 420, 160 + 120 + 140 = 420). 2) 57 + 37 + 38 = 132. Ones: 7 + 7 + 8 = 22, so write 2 and carry 2 tens. Tens: 5 + 3 + 3 + 2 = 13. The first box is 7 and the second box is 3. 3) No. Her check gives 533, not 523, so 266 is wrong. The right answer is 256 (ones: 13 − 7 = 6; tens: the 2 tens lent 1 ten to the ones, so 1 ten is left and we borrow again: 11 − 6 = 5; hundreds: 4 − 2 = 2). Check: 256 + 267 = 523. Mei’s tens digit is 1 too big: she forgot that the tens had already lent 1 ten to the ones. 4) (Question: True or false? Say how you know without working out both sides. (a) 346 + 199 = 345 + 200 (b) 270 + 130 = 260 + 150 (c) 618 + 99 = 600 + 117) (a) True: 346 is 1 more than 345 and 199 is 1 less than 200. (b) False: 270 is 10 more than 260, but 130 is 20 less than 150, so the sides are 400 and 410. (c) True: 618 is 18 more than 600 and 99 is 18 less than 117 (both sides are 717).

p2l2-challenge.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time). Pairs try first, then use the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. These are Think Harder Q5 and Q6. Answers: 1) 10 ways: 507 + 493, 517 + 483, 527 + 473, 537 + 463, 547 + 453, 557 + 443, 567 + 433, 577 + 423, 587 + 413, 597 + 403. 2) A 150, B 100, C 250.

p2l2-chdiag.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time). Show after pairs have tried the Go further, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Ask: Which column can you be sure about first? Will there be a carry? In Q2, compare two of the clues: what is the same, what is different? Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p2l2-chwalk.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time). Use after pairs have tried. Q1: list the tens pairs in order so none is missed: (0, 9), (1, 8) … (9, 0). Many children find a few and stop; ask "How do you know there are no more?" Q2: the same "take away the extra, halve" model as worksheet Q6. Guess and check also works: try 100 in Box A, then Box B has 150 and Box C has 200, but Box A and Box C together are only 300, too small, so Box A must have more.

p2l2-talk.note: Minutes 76.5 to 81.5. Pairs talk for 90 seconds, then two volunteers share. Answer: the ones can make a carry that changes the tens, and the tens can make a carry that changes the hundreds. So we must know the ones first. Praise the reasons, not only the answers. Talk time rules: you choose volunteers first ("Who would like to share?"); never cold-call a child by name; any child may say pass; no public tallies, scores or rankings.

p2l2-exit.note: Minutes 81.5 to 86.5. Answer: the box is 4 (344 + 257 = 601: ones 4 + 7 = 11, carry 1; tens 4 + 5 + 1 = 10, carry 1; hundreds 3 + 2 + 1 = 6). Bonus for anyone who would like it: 4[ ]6 + 37[ ] = 801 gives 2 in the first box and 5 in the second box (426 + 375 = 801). Extension: make your own missing-digit sum with two boxes and exactly one answer; swap with a partner. Children keep slips on their desks and tick them against the answer on the next click; nothing is held up. About 2 minutes of child work.

p2l2-reflect.note: Minutes 86.5 to 88.5. Looking back: about 2 minutes, in the box on the page called "Before you go: Investigation and Looking back" (the page after worksheet page 2; every child reaches it). Children finish one line, two lines or all three, and tick what helped. A pass is always allowed. No marks and no wrong answers. Tutor script: SAY: Looking back takes 2 minutes. Find the box called Looking back on the page “Before you go: Investigation and Looking back”. Finish one line, two lines or all three, and tick what helped you. You may pass on any line. If you tick "I am still stuck", your tutor will check in during the session. DO: Nothing is collected in front of the group and nobody has to read theirs out. The tutor may read a box while stamping journals (never by private message), and checks in on a child who ticked still stuck during the open session, for example by a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal with a parent nearby, for example "I saw you drew it when you got stuck". A child may volunteer one sentence, never by name unless they choose to. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the next open session (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby). Praise the strategy, not the speed. Closing and stamps take the last minute and a half (88.5 to 90).
